claims.text: Enhanced corrosion resistance in steels used for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a thin, continuous chromium oxide passivation film.
The baseline steels contain approximately 12-14% chromium.
The proposed study systematically varies chromium concentration in the steel.
Acid etching is used to remove or thin the naturally formed oxide layer before controlled reoxidation.
Samples are exposed to a chloride-rich aqueous environment at approximately 50°C for 72 hours under controlled oxygen conditions.
The governing structural mediator is a protective chromium oxide layer on the steel surface.
The protective surface layer consists primarily of Cr2O3.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes during environmental exposure.
Preferential chromium oxidation produces a stable and adherent Cr2O3 passive film.
The Cr2O3 film limits access of aggressive species such as chloride ions to the underlying metal.
Limiting aggressive-species access to the underlying metal retards further corrosion.
Steels with sufficiently enriched and intact chromium oxide films will have lower corrosion current densities than lower-chromium steels or steels with disturbed passive films.
Steels with sufficiently enriched and intact chromium oxide films will exhibit less weight loss than lower-chromium steels or steels with disturbed passive films.
Steels with sufficiently enriched and intact chromium oxide films will exhibit less surface pitting than lower-chromium steels or steels with disturbed passive films.
Baseline steels containing approximately 12-14% chromium form a naturally occurring but less robust passivation layer.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply within typical chromium-alloying ranges under moderate-temperature, chloride-containing aqueous conditions.
Very high temperatures, high pressures, or non-aqueous corrosive environments may introduce additional corrosion mechanisms.
Molybdenum, nickel, and microstructural features such as grain boundaries may contribute additional effects that are not isolated by the proposed study.
Failure to observe a statistically significant corrosion-rate decrease or improved film characteristics with increased chromium or intact passive films would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
